_comment: A deliberate departure from an inherited title. plerdy-titles.json is a record of someone else's checklist and stays faithful to it; when this plugin's evidence cannot answer the borrowed sentence, the local title is declared here with the reason it differs. Keys are registry item ids; keys beginning with _ are metadata and never reach the generator. An override that matches the source title is not a no-op, it is a dead entry - delete it.

CI-002.title: Confirm Google Has Indexed the Audited URL
CI-002.why: URL Inspection answers for one URL, and requires: gsc keeps the item out of the per-page sampled pass, so it answers for the audited URL only. The Plerdy wording 'Ensure Important Content Is Indexed' claims the site's important content. Checking a set of important URLs needs a quota-aware GSC sampling feature that does not exist, so the plugin must not keep a title that implies it. The wording also has to stay distinct from CI-001 'Ensure URL Is Indexed', which asks whether this page can be indexed rather than whether Google has.

TE-181.title: Validate the Rendered DOM (W3C)
TE-181.why: TE-181 now sends the browser-built DOM to the Nu checker, while CI-017 keeps validating the HTML served at the URL. Keeping the inherited title on both would give two report rows the same name even when the two documents produce different verdicts.

TE-169.title: Provide Internal Links in the Served HTML
TE-169.why: The inherited title — Optimize JavaScript Rendering & Crawlability — promises a comparison between the served document and the rendered one. That comparison is MB-105, and scoring it three times is what the duplicate gate exists to stop. This item asserts something real and cheap about the served document, and its independently written fixture declaration already says so: every sampled page carries internal links in the served HTML. The title is brought into line with what both the assertion and the declaration mean.

LO-200.title: Publish Complete NAP in LocalBusiness Data
LO-200.why: The inherited title promises two off-site facts that a fetched page cannot establish: a business can have a complete Google Business Profile without linking it from the page, and visible on-page reviews are not evidence of its off-site review presence. LO-198 already asks whether LocalBusiness data exists anywhere on the site; this item grades the page-level fact the fetched data can prove: every LocalBusiness node present has a non-empty name, address and telephone.

MB-105.title: Ensure Content, Meta & Directives Match Between Served and Rendered HTML
MB-105.why: The inherited title promises mobile-versus-desktop parity, but nothing in this plugin measures that. javascript_render_audit.py takes one URL and one operator-supplied rendered artifact; it has no concept of a user agent, viewport or second serve, and compares the served document with that artifact across title, meta description, canonical, H1 count, internal-link count, schema count and word count. Calling the rendered side Desktop sends the operator looking for user-agent switching when the finding is a JavaScript rendering gap. TE-169 and TE-177 already identify MB-105 as this served-versus-rendered comparison; this override makes MB-105 say the same from its side.

MD-184.title: Confirm the Page References at Least One Image
MD-184.why: The inherited title — Audit Sitewide Image Usage — promises a reading of how a whole site uses images, and this item is `image_inventory.py` over one fetched URL asserting `count gte 1`: it says the served HTML of one page names at least one image with a `src`, and nothing about how the site uses images anywhere else. The gap is not only in scope. Since 0.49.0 `image_inventory.py` withholds `count` from a page carrying no image, so an image-free page is undecided rather than failing and `count` is `len(rows)` whenever it is present: PASS and NO_DATA are the item's whole vocabulary, and the `medium` FAIL this item once produced on the exemplary fixture was the defect 0.49.0 repaired. It answered PASS on all five trees this repository can serve, `tests/corpus/failing-shapes/` — built to fail as much as a static server can express — included. A title promising an audit therefore names a judgement the item as it stands cannot deliver. `References` rather than `Uses`, because the assertion proves the markup names an image and never that one loads. The assertion is left where it is: what a sitewide reading would assert is a registry question that moves live verdicts, and this release only stops the title claiming to be one.

TE-177.title: Provide a Title Element in the Served HTML
TE-177.why: The inherited title — Ensure No-JS Access & Crawlability — promises a comparison between the served document and the rendered one. That comparison is MB-105, and scoring it three times is what the duplicate gate exists to stop. This item asserts something real and cheap about the served document, and its independently written fixture declaration already says so: every sampled page carries a title element in the served HTML. The title is brought into line with what both the assertion and the declaration mean.

GO-143.title: Complete Every WebSite Node Google Reads for the Site Name
GO-143.why: The inherited title — Optimize for Sitelinks & Sitelinks Search Box — names two things this item cannot deliver, and one of them no longer exists. Sitelinks are algorithmic: Google publishes no markup that produces them, so no assertion here can optimise for them. The Sitelinks Search Box did rest on `WebSite` `potentialAction`/`SearchAction`, and Google removed it from Search starting 21 November 2024 — globally, in every language, and out of Search Console and the Rich Results Test with it. Until 0.89.0 this item failed any page whose `WebSite` node lacked that markup, which asked the operator to publish a `SearchAction` naming a search endpoint the site may not have: a false statement about the site, made to earn a result that can no longer appear. What the assertion still measures is real and current — `WebSite` is what Google reads for the site name in results, and its documentation lists `name` and `url` as the required properties, which is exactly what `schema_required_props.py` requires of the type. The title says *every* node rather than *provide* one, and the difference is the item's real boundary: the assertion is per node and passes vacuously when a page declares no `WebSite` node at all. `Provide Complete WebSite Data for the Site Name` was the first attempt and an independent reader was right to call it a promise the item does not keep — an imperative to publish something reads as a check that it exists, and this item never fails on absence. `Complete Every …` is true either way: every node present carries a name and a url, and a page with none satisfies that without being asked for anything. `alternateName` is documented by Google as optional and is deliberately not asked for.

TE-179.title: Review Domain Registration History
TE-179.why: The inherited title — Review Domain History & Reputation — names two subjects and the assertion reaches one: `whois.age_days >= 90`. Reputation is asserted on the same script by SE-114, SE-116 and TE-171, all three on `safe_browsing.threats`, and `tools/audit_item_semantics.py` has recorded TE-179 as FIXED (0.44) on exactly that ground since then. Anton ruled on 21 September 2026 that a group of items does not close one item's title: REG-6 says the rule attached to an item shall decide the question that item's title asks, and a reader of the report sees this row alone. So the title is brought down to the half this item measures. `Registration History` rather than `History`, because whois age is when the domain was registered and not what was served from it — an archive of past content would be a different instrument, and the narrower word stops this title promising one.
